title: Four remediation proposals
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Four People Ops teams found the same problem: manager hierarchy is stale for a few hundred employees whose manager has left. All four are proposing to use AI on it.

**One of them keeps AI on the detection side and never lets it touch the correction.** Find it.

artifacts.label: Proposal A
artifacts.body: "We'll run a query to list every employee whose manager record is terminated, and have the model cross-reference the org structure, cost centre, and last three approval routings to propose the most likely correct manager for each — with a confidence score. Anything above 90% confidence we apply automatically overnight; below that goes to a person. That gets us through roughly 80% of the backlog without human time, and we keep the confidence threshold under review."

artifacts.label: Proposal B
artifacts.body: "The model produces a candidate list: one row per affected employee, the terminated manager, and the reason it was flagged — no proposed replacement, because that's a decision about who someone reports to. Bhavana reviews the list, samples 30 rows looking for whole categories of false positive rather than individual mistakes, and routes each row to the relevant HRBP for the actual reporting-line decision. We apply in batches of 50, we reversed one batch deliberately as a rehearsal (took nine minutes), and after each batch we check that the number of records changed equals the number approved."

artifacts.label: Proposal C
artifacts.body: "We're having the model generate the corrected hierarchy in full and output it as a load file. Before loading, two analysts independently review the complete file against the current org chart and sign off. It's 340 rows so a full review is feasible — we're not sampling, we're checking everything, which is stronger than a sample. Then one bulk load, one effective date, and it's done in a single evening rather than dragging across a quarter."

artifacts.label: Proposal D
artifacts.body: "First we're fixing the root cause: the offboarding process doesn't trigger a reporting-line reassignment, so we're adding a mandatory step and a validation rule that blocks a termination from completing until direct reports are reassigned. That stops new occurrences. For the existing 340, the model drafts a summary of the backlog by business unit and we hand it to each HRBP to work through in their next 1:1 cycle. No bulk change at all."

reasoning:
**B is the module's discipline, complete.** A candidate list with a reason per row and **deliberately no proposed replacement**, because who someone reports to is a decision about a person and belongs to a human with standing to make it. Then every element of the operational form: a real sample looking for **families** of false positive rather than individual errors, batches small enough to reverse, **a reversal actually rehearsed with the time recorded**, and a reconciliation of records-changed against records-approved after each batch.

Notice what B declines to do. It has the information required to guess the right manager and it does not guess, because the value of a correct guess is small and the cost of a confident wrong one is an employee reporting to a stranger — with approvals, reviews, and pay decisions flowing through that line. **That restraint is the whole lesson.**

**A is the trap, and it is seductive because the engineering is good.** Cross-referencing org structure, cost centre and approval history is exactly what a model is useful for. The failure is the last step: **applying above a confidence threshold, automatically, overnight.** Three things go wrong at once. Confidence is not accuracy — it correlates with fluency, and a model is most confident where the pattern is clean rather than where the answer is right. The 10% of cases below the threshold are the *easy* ones to catch; the dangerous ones are the confidently wrong. And overnight bulk application is Module 1's wide-reach long-latency quadrant precisely: it propagates to approvals and reporting before anyone reads a row. "We keep the threshold under review" reviews the wrong variable.

**C is the interesting failure, because it looks more rigorous than B and is less safe.** Two analysts reviewing all 340 rows *sounds* stronger than sampling 30. It isn't, for a reason worth internalising: **human attention degrades across rows.** Row 300 gets a fraction of the care row 3 got, both reviewers degrade in the same direction, and independence does not help when the failure mode is shared inattention. Sampling for *categories* of error finds a systematic fault that a fatigued full review misses. And then the ending undoes whatever the review achieved — **one bulk load, one effective date** is unreversible in practice, and "done in a single evening rather than dragging across a quarter" is schedule pressure written into the design.

**D is not wrong and is not an answer to the question asked.** Fixing the offboarding trigger is genuinely the best thing on this page — it stops new occurrences, and a validation rule is worth more than any remediation. Any real programme should do D *and* B. But as a proposal for the existing 340 it quietly abandons them to an HRBP 1:1 cycle with no owner, no date, and no completion check, and "the model drafts a summary by business unit" is the least valuable available use of AI here. **Prevention plus abandonment is still abandonment**, and the 340 dead approval chains stay dead.

The transferable test: **find the step where a record changes, and ask who approved that specific row.** In B, a named human did. In A, a threshold did. In C, a fatigued reviewer nominally did and a bulk load actually did. In D, nobody, ever.
